channel.title: It Will Not Leave
channel.description: Posts in the discussion thread "It Will Not Leave" - A grieved MTF officer cannot let his dead squadmate go

item.title: Re: It Will Not Leave
item.content:encoded:
Got a PM about this, stated I didn't like it and my review would be negative, was requested to look at this all the same. With that noted, here we go:

+ show block
– hide block

I'll be honest, I was rather immediately skeptical when I read that Adam and Samuel not only are childhood friends and joined police academy at the same time, but they were also recruited by the Foundation and placed on an MTF immediately. MTF agents are the Foundation's best of the best, and the teams are specialized for more than just generic combat—how on earth did both of these guys just immediately get put on an MTF team, let alone the same team?

The grief and sense of guilt pursuits Samuel to the point that starts to see Adam during his routine more often with time, to the point that jeopardizes other companions during some MTF operations. After a psychological test, he is given an amnestic to forget about his friend and stick to the MTF.

This is where I as a reader start to lose interest in a full draft of this. It strikes me as odd that no one bothered addressing Samuel's trauma until after he started jeopardizing operations—surely the Foundation would have had him attend counseling as soon as he returned from the original mission? The "psychological test" involving the amnestic just seems incompetent and negligent; even if Samuel asked for his memory to be erased, he shouldn't have been allowed to continue with his MTF duties. It's also a huge hit to Task Force morale if the way the Foundation handles grief is to just force people to forget and chuck them back into the field.

However, after some time without issues, during an intense MTF operation, Samuel provokes a containment breach as he claims that an unknown individual appeared to him.

At this point the plotline just feels too contrived for me to take it seriously. Given the Foundation's judgment lapses thus far, as a reader I react with more "well, what did they expect?" and not "oh no, that's terrible!"

Foundation demotes him and keeps him a study subject in order to prevent further failed operations, classifying Adam’s apparition as an SCP object.

I mean, I guess after two ill-advised doses of amnestics it's reasonable to guess that something anomalous is afoot, but I'm still wondering why Samuel didn't get any sort of therapeutic care during all of this.

Eventually, Samuel commits suicide.

I would downvote pretty immediately for this. It's overdramatic and entirely avoidable, and the usage of suicide as a plot point doesn't sit well with me. Granted, I myself headcanon the Foundation as extremely competent… if you really want to write a story where the Foundation thoroughly fails to help one of their personnel, I'm definitely not the right reviewer for such a piece.

An MTF operative from Samuel’s former MTF squad is recorded in a tapped phone call claiming that he has spotted Samuel in his garden and is afraid of reporting this to the Foundation.

Why would this MTF agent be scared of reporting that sighting? The Foundation can't do anything about what they don't know, and keeping knowledge of a potential anomalous effect secret would put everyone else the operative works with at risk.

Adam’s apparition to Samuel is not real. It is driven by strong feelings of guilt, grief and melancholy. […] So to avoid jeopardizing future operations, Foundation classifies it as an anomaly. Samuel’s sorrow becomes a memetic effect.

I have a very difficult time taking this seriously. Emotions and mental symptoms associated with traumatic events are very real and I can't see the Foundation treating this case as an anomaly. The justification of "they don't want to jeopardize future operations" doesn't make sense (unless Samuel is just too irreplaceable) since Samuel wouldn't mess up operations if he was allowed to take time away to mourn in peace. The sorrow becoming a memetic effect also seems odd since there's no specific information being transferred here. Mind-affecting maybe, but I'm not seeing the memetics relation.

It also seems weird that the Foundation would decide to write up an uncontainable anomalous phenomenon that would cause more panic, rather than just getting the MTF staff some therapy.

First, how even long-term friendship can deeply mark an individual;

This admittedly makes me curious as to why Adam and Samuel were placed on the same MTF team. They'd potential be emotional liabilities to each other. I can see why it has to be set up this way to commence the desired plot, but if the narrative focus on friendship is reliant on a contrived plot, the emotion might feel artificial and disingenuous.

and second, the HRM policy of the Foundation regarding its MTF operatives, and the perils of mental health mismanagement.

Given that the MTF agents are the best of the best, I have trouble believing that the Foundation would mismanage Samuel's care to such a disastrous degree. Again, the incompetence of the Foundation feels more like authorial meddling than something that I personally would believe, and the core theme is difficult for me to take seriously as currently presented.

As an aside, I admittedly have a lot of skepticism on this sort of story since I've volunteered at a psyc department, written a thesis on cancer patient trauma, and handled data for for a stress research lab. There's a wide body of research regarding grief and mourning (also one of my best friends lost a beloved dog recently. She says she still hears his barking sometimes. This isn't an abnormality) and the main roadblock I have is the Foundation being portrayed as, well… pretty clueless, it seems.

Again though, I tend to be more picky and demanding for scientific realism than most readers. There are plenty community members who enjoy stories where the Foundation messes up a lot; I just personally can't take those stories seriously enough to enjoy the read.

So far as suggestions for moving forward go, this is what I recommend:

  • change the role assignment for the two. MTF raises more eyebrows than, say, security personnel (would make sense for someone with police work in their resume) or field agent.
  • have the Foundation provide therapy for Samuel after Adam dies.
  • make it clear that Samuel asks to be put on the amnestics. Have it just be the one dose.
  • don't have the Foundation write up the anomaly. Maybe have the document be something that Samuel was writing up himself, believing that he was affected by an anomaly because his grief broke through the amnestics.
  • don't end the piece with Samuel's suicide.
  • if you want to have the Foundation be really struggling to provide mental health care, have there be a clear and believable reason why. Remote site that is dangerous and inhospitable to therapists who are used to working in offices? Stubborn refusal of Samuel to take the counseling sessions seriously? Etc.

I myself would have set this up as a tale. Do you really need to have this be an SCP article? You can consider writing a tale that has article inserts, like Revised Entry or Reality Check.

item.title: Re: It Will Not Leave
item.content:encoded:
Whoa, that was amazing. Thank you so much for such an extensive feedback. I will answer it without any order:

+ Some notes incoming
- Go
  • I agree with the Foundation attitude to the problem not being 'saving money'. I think the obvious approach would instead be that it would be risky to keep the guy in the MTF squad, as it might keep endangering other squad mates due to his unpredictability. As the situation escalates and Samuel is emotionally stopped from performing any activity, that would be another reason to separate him from the group. (edited in the OP)
  • I did not know about MTF Omega-0. I have not read thoroughly about it yet, but my understanding is that it uploads 'memories' to the SCP intranet? I might believe that if Samuel is troubled in his mind, syncing his mind/soul/spirit to the Foundation intranet might actually threaten the stability of Omega-0. It could even act as a cybervirus for the performance of the Omega-0 squad.
  • I understand that telling this story either as a Tale or SCP entails radically different structures. I can state two arguments why I think I would prefer to write this as an SCP file.
    • First, as a newbie writer I am not that confident yet on my strength in fully fleshing-out feelings of this kind in a Tale, without sounding exaggerated or hyperbolic. I am absolutely into subtlety, which ties with my second argument.
    • As you mentioned, one of the reasons why I did not write Adam's apparition to be real (aside from the mental health topic) is to play with the reader's expectations. Despite the clinical approach by the Foundation, the reader would nonetheless think that something is off. If we are telling the reader every time that Samuel is watching someone, she would be more prone to think that Samuel's right while the Foundation is missing something. As story progresses, amnestics result powerless and Samuel becomes physically constrained due to his mental strings, and so the reader would confirm her expectations.
    • One of the consequences of the SCP format is that the reader would actually never know if Adam's apparition was actually real or not. But I find that attractive, though. In this case, I think it would better work that the Foundation considers anomalous not 'Adam's apparition', but Samuel's mental problem, due to the resistance to amnestics.
    • Samuel's image becoming a memetic effect is something I am not quite sure, honestly. It may appear out of the blue, but it is another plot twist that I guess one does not see coming. If at all, one might expect Adam to appear to another MTF officer, not Samuel. But it might change the meaning of the whole writing by emphasizing the idea of Samuel's sorrow. Also, it rises the stakes for the Foundation, as it implies that what happened to Samuel might 'jump' to MTF officers and affect them, risking prospective MTF operations. The Foundation might establish as containment procedure that MTFs are to be monitored in case somebody shows any of the mentioned effects, isolate the guy to confirm it, and keep it alive for the time being.
  • The idea I explained as 'Central Narrative' was intended to stand as background: it would be told as you mention via medical/psychological reports, video logs from the missions, etc. Specifically, I had in mind to include one file acting as a HRM initial report at the moment of entry of Samuel; and another file being an interview with Adam and Samuel's mentor in police academy detailing their closeness. This second one could be included into the HRM initial report as well.
  • On Samuel's suicide, I understand it is a sensitive topic and difficult to pull off. The final twist requires him to die to make sense. A final addendum stating that Samuel appeared dead in his cell, then tying up with him appearing to another MTF officer seems too simple and anticlimactic. A suicide note seems also unconvincing and unoriginal, not to mention that he was reportedly unable to perform any action by that time.

That was a long response, I think I did not miss anything. Again, thank you so much for your help!

item.title: Re: It Will Not Leave
item.content:encoded:
This…is a really strong newbie concept.

Okay. Warning. Rambley crit ahead. So please.

+Bear with me
-Yeet

I adore the emotional aspect and I'm a sucker for…how should I put it? 'Dead spirit super attached to living person' stories? Best way to put it?

I do have issues, though. First off…the topic of suicide. It's a difficult topic to handle, as it's extremely sensitive and one needs to pull it off well in order to make it work. I really like what you have here in concept, but I'm worried about the execution.

Also, go here
http://www.scpwiki.com/task-forces#omega-0

And look at the Mobile Task Force called MTF Omega-0 ("Ará Orún"). In summary, it's a Mobile Task Force comprised of the spirits(?) of dead Foundation personnel.

Note: SCP Foundation storytelling is allheadcanon, so you don't have to do anything with this MTF, but I figured someone would mention it later down the road, so I figured you'd need to know.

Also, I get it's just a hallucination and not actually a spirit, but still. I just wanted to share that MTF.

My last question is this: tell me why this needs to be an SCP and not a Tale.

A Tale, you have so much freedom to tell a story however you choose.

An SCP with its restrictive post-mortem emotionless scientific document format, the best way I can see this being told is a combination of interviews, handwritten notes, video footage of the MTFs behavior, perhaps some examples of on the field mission logs where the grieving MTF soldier starts losing his cool and goes nuts. That can all work perfectly, I admit but I'd want to see how you'd portray it.

In a Tale, you can accurately describe everything down to the nitty gritty of the MTF seeing his dead mate and such.

In the SCP format, all you'd be showing is someone going nuts from an outsider's perspective. The only anomalous bit would be the kicker in an addendum that someone else started hallucinating it.

Both have their strengths but I just want you to be aware of what storytelling tools you have.

Now, one final issue I have. This is a grave one. Extremely grave issue.

In benefit of maintaining resources, rather than promoting an adequate mental health, Foundation classifies it as an anomaly and moves on.

I don't see money as an issue to the Foundation. Also, this person's Mobile Task Force. I don't really buy them just shrugging him off like that.

The 'not an anomaly but emotions turn it into an anomaly' bit, I see working just fine. If anything, this can toy with the reader's expectations and make them wonder whether it really is a ghost or just a hallucination.

The careless attitude of the Foundation, I don't buy. Besides, I imagine they have on site mental health experts.

I don't know, maybe have him be checked out repeatedly by mental health experts and then have it fail and then have it be classified as an anomaly afterwards? After he commits suicide (which you'll still need to find a way to execute well.)

Simply saying 'screw it' and classifying an anomaly out of desire to save funds is so not Foundation.

Anywho, that ends my incredibly rambley crit. I apologise if some of this was a little unclear. If you need clarification, feel free to PM me.

I hope I helped and I bid you a lovely day.

👍

item.title: It Will Not Leave
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Horror, Drama/Emotional

Page Layout (Optional): Interviews and incident logs to be included.

Elevator Pitch: : An MTF officer starts to spot in random situations a former squad companion who died in an earlier Containment operation. Despite Foundation help with amnestics, the visions become more frequent and intense.

Central Narrative: Adam and Samuel have been friends since nursery times: they attended the same high school and joined the police academy at the same time. After some time in a police station, they are recruited by the SCP Foundation to join a MTF. Some years later, during a Containment operation, Samuel fails to follow protocol and ends up with Adam dead. The grief and sense of guilt pursuits Samuel to the point that starts to see Adam during his routine more often with time, to the point that jeopardizes other companions during some MTF operations. After a psychological test, he is given an amnestic to forget about his friend and stick to the MTF.

+ show block
– hide block

However, after some time without issues, during an intense MTF operation, Samuel provokes a containment breach as he claims that an unknown individual appeared to him. This appearance will never leave from then on. After providing a description to the psychologist, matching that of Adam, he is given another amnestic. The entity does not disappear though, and it starts to directly intervene in Adam’s actions, deterring him from any basic activity. Foundation demotes him and keeps him a study subject in order to prevent further failed operations, classifying Adam’s apparition as an SCP object. Eventually, Samuel commits suicide. An MTF operative from Samuel’s former MTF squad is recorded in a tapped phone call claiming that he has spotted Samuel in his garden and is afraid of reporting this to the Foundation.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: Adam’s apparition to Samuel is not real. It is driven by strong feelings of guilt, grief and melancholy. The abnormality comes from the exaggerated expression of these feelings, which get so stuck to Samuel and his subconscious that even amnestics cannot fully support Samuel. So to avoid jeopardizing future operations, Foundation classifies it as an anomaly. Samuel’s sorrow becomes a memetic effect.

Additional Notes: There are two main ideas that I wanted to explore. First, how even long-term friendship can deeply mark an individual; and second, the HRM policy of the Foundation regarding its MTF operatives, and the perils of mental health mismanagement.
